analysis.one_liner: Lets states pool federal health dollars into their own universal, publicly run coverage plans.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has seen no action since its July 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add a new waiver to the Affordable Care Act letting a state apply to combine the federal health dollars its residents already draw — from Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, federal employee and military coverage, and employer-plan rules — into one state-run universal health plan. The state must cover everyone, keep benefits at least as comprehensive and affordable as the federal programs it replaces, guarantee reproductive and gender-affirming care, and reach 95% coverage within five years or risk losing the waiver. It is optional: nothing changes in any state unless that state enacts its own law and applies.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of any state that opts in, especially the uninsured and people with thin or expensive coverage, who would get a publicly administered plan covering everyone regardless of job or income. States gain flexibility to reinvest any administrative savings into health services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: A state that wins a waiver receives, as a lump sum with caseload growth and health-inflation adjustments, the federal funds that would otherwise have been spent on Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA tax credits, and federal employee and military coverage for its residents [S2].

The state plan must cover all residents, match or beat the comprehensiveness and affordability of the federal programs it replaces, guarantee coverage for reproductive health care including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care, and be publicly administered [S2].
Any savings from running the programs — including administrative savings — stay with the state for reinvestment in health care services [S2].

Applications are public: notice and comment, disclosure of what laws the state seeks to waive, annual reports to Congress, and an independent panel including patient advocates, nurses, and rural and primary-care clinicians that reviews every application [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If a state adopts it, state taxpayers would have to cover any gap between the federal passthrough and the plan's cost, since the bill requires the arrangement to be budget-neutral for the federal government. Private health insurers in that state would lose most of their core coverage market, though states may contract with private firms to administer the plan and may allow supplemental policies for benefits the state plan does not cover.

drawbacks.text: The waiver must be budget-neutral for the federal government over a 10-year plan, so the state itself would have to raise the money for anything the passthrough does not cover — meaning state taxes or fees [S2].
A state must reach coverage for at least 95% of its residents within five years; after a 12-month grace period, the Secretary may terminate the waiver if it falls short [S2].

The state plan may restrict the sale of private insurance that duplicates its benefits, and the state would provide public education about those restrictions — people who prefer private coverage would lose that option for the benefits the state plan covers [S2].
A state can repeal its law and terminate the waiver, and each state's plan would differ, so coverage would not be uniform across the country [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is large for residents of a participating state — everyone covered, no job or income gatekeeping, cost-sharing floors that beat current federal programs. The costs are real but mostly pushed to the state level: the state must fund any shortfall and meet a demanding 95% coverage target under penalty of losing the waiver. The design includes public review, independent evaluation, and an exit for states that repeal their law, which limits the risk of a poorly run plan persisting. The main weakness is that it solves nothing nationally — it only opens a door for states willing and able to finance their own universal systems.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it; no vote has been taken.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on July 15, 2025, joined by Sens. Warren, Merkley, and Padilla [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been recorded since the referral [S4].
Three Democratic senators have cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, the existing system stands: private health insurers keep the coverage market, and no state can yet use this pathway to set up universal coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All four Senate sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats — 4 of the 45 Senate Democrats — with no Republican support, and the bill sits with the Republican-led Finance Committee.

industries.note: In participating states, a publicly administered plan covering everyone would displace most individual, employer, Medicaid-managed-care, and Medicare Advantage business. The bill does leave insurers two roles: states may contract private entities to administer the state plan, and supplemental policies can still be sold for benefits the state plan does not cover [S2].

The waiver list includes ERISA's preemption rule, so a state could fold employer plans into its universal plan. Employers who now fund coverage could pay less in premiums but would face state financing instead; employees would trade employer plan design for a public plan.

A single payer in a participating state means one payment system instead of dozens of insurers, cutting billing overhead — but the bill does not set payment rates, so whether providers gain or lose revenue depends entirely on the state's plan.

analysis.trajectory: With a 55-seat Republican Senate majority, no Republican cosponsors, and referral to the Finance Committee in July 2025 with no action since, the realistic path is that the bill stays in committee and dies when this Congress ends in January 2027. A single-state pilot of this kind could only advance if a future Congress or committee leadership chose to act on it.
